items.body:
Providing a future-proof source of electricity and contributing to lower CO₂ emissions, power produced from biomass is increasingly economically viable. The interests of operators and investors, on the one hand, and those of utilities and grids, on the other, are becoming more closely aligned. This is because ensuring a stable power supply as well as the financial success of the power plant are common goals.

The biorefinery will be the first industrial-scale facility of its type ever built. It will apply novel process innovations to sustainably convert 100 percent wood into bio-based mono-ethylene glycol (MEG), mono-propylene glycol (MPG) as well as renewable functional fillers (RFF).

With more widespread environmental awareness and the resultant striving for “green” lifestyles, biomass energy for both industry and electricity providers is a reliable – and sustainable – source of baseload power.

It also helps in meeting environmental targets, absorbing more CO₂ than it emits, and efficient equipment used in power generation leads to fewer emissions at the plant site.

Biomass is a relatively cheap base load and, depending on the local regulations, surplus electricity produced from it can be fed back to the grid, making it even more economically viable.

Installing a biomass power plant to burn the on-site waste that occurs as a by-product of industrial processes closes the factory input cycle.

It also eliminates the need for waste disposal, lowers energy costs and maintains a high availability of the power supply.

Incinerating renewables is thus a further step toward sustainability and toward a closed-cycle economy. These by-products need no additional processing, further strengthening the financial feasibility of the biomass plant.

The possibility of running a biomass plant on diverse feedstocks adds to the viability of such projects while ensuring the availability of the fuel supply.

Apart from achieving maximum output with a minimum of life-cycle costs, another decisive economic factor is the need for appropriate frameworks already in the country concerned, regulating such variables as electricity prices, the level of tipping tax, and funding.

With their leading efficiency profile and minimal outages, our turbines maximize the amount of electricity generated while further reducing a plant’s lifetime emissions footprint.

All our turbines offer a long life cycle thanks to reliable equipment that is backed by our global service.

Thanks to our long list of references we can help gain acceptance for biomass energy among the authorities and the local population.

We can support you from the very beginning with our technical consulting and expertise, dealing with all the parties involved and avoiding any complications.

Industries producing a large amount of process (biomass) waste can convert it into carbon-neutral energy to power their facilities or sell into the grid for additional revenue.

items.title: Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS)
items.description: Discover innovative Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) technology. Learn how CCUS is crucial for reducing CO₂ emissions for a sustainable future.
items.familyLabel: Usecase Carbon Capture Utilization And Storage

faqs.q: What is carbon capture?
faqs.a: CCS is a technology that aims to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) levels by capturing CO₂ from industrial processes and power generation, thereby preventing it from contributing to climate change. The captured CO₂ is then transported to safe storage sites and sequestered underground in geological formations to ensure it does not re-enter the atmosphere.

faqs.q: Why is carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) important?
faqs.a: A wide range of technologies and strategies are needed to tackle climate change and achieve net-zero emissions. CCUS stands out as a critical technology in this mission, providing a key solution to significantly reduce (CO₂) emissions while maintaining the use of critical energy infrastructure. CCUS involves capturing carbon dioxide from sources such as power plants and either reusing or storing them to prevent them from entering the atmosphere.

faqs.q: What is the difference between CCUS and CCS?
faqs.a: The difference between CCUS and CCS lies in the utilization aspect. While CCS focuses solely on the capture and storage of CO₂, CCUS involves the use of the captured CO₂ in various industries, turning it into a valuable commodity.

faqs.q: How is Siemens Energy working on CCUS?
faqs.a: At Siemens Energy, we are committed to advancing CCUS technologies through strategic partnerships and by leveraging our extensive experience in the power industry. Our capabilities extend beyond the core power plant infrastructure, where we can also offer integration of carbon capture equipment into existing and new facilities to ensure optimal performance. Our portfolio elements are broad and include compression and liquefaction solutions, control and automation solutions. In addition, our extensive experience as a service provider enables us to offer a comprehensive range of service solutions tailored to the specific needs of our customers.

items.body:
At Siemens Energy, we believe in the potential of Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS). Advancing this technology is essential for a sustainable future. By partnering with customers, CCUS providers, and policymakers, we lead in decarbonizing the energy sector. Together, we are building a more sustainable world for future generations. Let’s turn ambition into action and create a cleaner, greener planet.

To effectively combat climate change and reach net-zero emissions, a multitude of technologies are essential. CCUS will play a pivotal role in reducing CO₂ emissions by leveraging existing infrastructure. The International Energy Agency (IEA) underscores the necessity of CCUS, emphasizing the need to capture approximately 1 gigatonne of CO₂ annually by 2030 to align with international climate objectives, such as those set by the Paris Agreement. Integration design studies are important in refining CO₂ capture plants in terms of size, cost, and efficiency. Our equipment, including steam and gas compressors, facilitates CCUS deployment across the entire spectrum, encompassing capture, storage, and utilization. The process of capturing CO₂ after combustion is notably energy-demanding, relying on electricity and low-pressure steam usually sourced from the power plant, which can diminish the plant's overall efficiency and power output. By optimizing steam turbine configurations and harnessing waste heat from CO₂ capture and compression, we can improve the power plant output, efficiency, and functionality of these plants.

CCUS can be added to new build or be retrofitted to existing fossil fuel-based power plants and industrial facilities, capturing CO₂ emissions that would otherwise be released into the atmosphere. This is particularly important for sectors where emissions are hard to abate, such as cement and steel production.

Hydrogen is a clean fuel that can be produced using fossil fuels with CCUS, known as blue hydrogen. This process captures the CO₂ produced during hydrogen production, making it a low-carbon alternative to green hydrogen produced from renewable energy sources until enough resources for green hydrogen are constructed.

CCUS technologies can also capture CO₂ directly with direct air capture (DAC) or from bioenergy processes (BECCS). These methods can remove CO₂ from the atmosphere, helping to balance emissions that are difficult to eliminate. Furthermore the synergistic approach of Direct Air Capture combined with carbon sequestration (DACCS) is acknowledged for its potential to generate negative emissions, representing a robust, enduring approach to Carbon Dioxide Removal.

In addition to our comprehensive approach to Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS), we are also focusing on the system design aspects, including liquefication and drying. These processes are crucial for the efficient handling and storage of captured CO₂. Liquefication allows for the CO₂ to be transported more easily and stored in a more compact form, while drying ensures that the CO₂ is free from moisture, which can cause corrosion and other issues in storage and transportation systems.

The global energy landscape largely relies on fossil fuels, by 2035, DNV estimates ~30% of electricity will still come from fossil fuels (Energy Transition Outlook 2024). An abrupt switch to renewables is not yet feasible. CCUS-equipped gas-fired power generation complements renewable energy, ensuring availability and security when renewables are offline. We are leading in the development of CCUS technology, addressing climate change and supporting the transition to a low-carbon future.

We have explored carbon management technologies for decades and continue to find ways to support the energy sector's transition with CCUS. Our extensive knowledge of energy systems allows us to work with industry partners to integrate carbon capture technology and create comprehensive CCUS solutions.

Different technologies cater to various industries' needs, addressing their specific emission sources and regulatory environments. We collaborate with leading carbon capture providers to deliver efficient, reliable customized solutions.

Our strategic partnerships, combined with our extensive experience in energy technology, enable us to access cutting-edge technologies from leading suppliers. This allows us to concentrate on our core competency of integrating power plants with capture plants, thereby ensuring optimal efficiency and asset utilization.

Discover how Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage helps achieve net-zero emissions and the needed infrastructure.

CCUS is a key technological innovation aimed at reducing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. By capturing CO₂ from industrial processes, air and power and heat generation, CCUS prevents this greenhouse gas from impacting climate change. The captured CO₂ is then either repurposed in various industries or safely stored underground. CCUS is essential for lowering emissions in challenging sectors like steel and cement manufacturing and is a complement of sustainable low-carbon electricity and hydrogen production. As a method for atmospheric CO₂ removal, CCUS is integral to achieving net-zero emissions and ensuring long-term energy security.

Advanced capture technologies such as pre-combustion, post-combustion, DAC and oxy-fuel combustion of CO₂ from the atmosphere are employed to intercept CO₂ emissions at their source, including industrial and power generation facilities.

Once captured, CO₂ can be put to work in various sectors, being used in the chemical, and food and beverage industries, thus turning a waste product into a valuable commodity.

Transportation to secure storage locations and subsequent underground sequestration of CO₂ in geological formations ensures that it is contained and does not re-enter the atmosphere.

CCUS offers significant potential for a sustainable future. Although high costs, infrastructure needs, and regulatory uncertainties pose challenges, they also drive innovation. Government support, such as tax credits and carbon pricing, can spur progress. Additionally, international collaboration and investment in R&D are essential for advancing CCUS technologies, enhancing their efficiency and cost-effectiveness.

Embracing these opportunities will promote CCUS adoption, cut carbon emissions, and support a sustainable planet.

As a trusted partner, we help our customers select the most appropriate technologies for their specific needs. By partnering with leading carbon capture providers, we combine our energy technology and infrastructure expertise with their specialized knowledge to deliver efficient and reliable customized solutions.

items.title: Coal-to-Gas Conversion for Power Plants
items.description: Convert coal plants to efficient gas to cut CO₂ emissions by up to 70%. Use existing assets now and prepare for future hydrogen adoption.

faqs.q: Step 1: Design concept
faqs.a: Understanding customer’s market environment, the regional energy system and regulatory framework in order to create a customized cost-optimized, efficient, or flexible solution, while aiming at the same time at integrating as many existing assets as possible.

faqs.q: Step 2: Geometrical fit
faqs.a: Analyzing how to integrate the new equipment – such as gas turbines or generators – fit into the existing plant layout and infrastructure. Especially for indoor solutions, it’s important to analyze how existing foundations, piping and connections can be reused, while ensuring the new setup will work smoothly and safely.

faqs.q: Step 3: Thermodynamic fit
faqs.a: Identifying the best configuration with the best thermodynamic fit in order to match the future operating regime with the intended business model. This can involve various, far-reaching measures, as, e.g., the steam cycle of a conventional steam power plant differs fundamentally from that of a CCPP.

faqs.q: Step 4: Steam turbine retrofit
faqs.a: Adapting the existing steam turbine and generator to operating parameters of a combined cycle plant. This may concern especially higher temperatures – up to 600°C and more for a steam turbine – that modern CCPPs use today.

items.body:
75% of global CO₂ emissions in the power generation sector are caused by coal power plants. Converting coal-fired power plants into highly efficient combined cycle plants can reduce CO2 emissions by up to 70%. It also gives you the option to co-fire clean hydrogen in your gas turbine, enabling you to decarbonize your plant operation even further.

Based on the Brownfield Transformation concept, our approach includes repurposing as much of your existing infrastructure as possible to enable a fast transition towards a new energy system while reducing CO₂ emissions at the same time.

A full repowering entails not just changing the fuel from coal or oil to gas but converting the steam power plant to a highly efficient combined cycle power plant (CCPP) by reusing infrastructure, site permits and local personnel. Not only is this approach faster and more sustainable but it also saves up to 30% of Capex compared to building a new power plant.

There are two options to repower your plant: the indoor and the outdoor approach.

With the indoor approach, you can reuse most of the existing infrastructure such as foundations, connections, housing and piping. This saves time and costs. With the outdoor approach, you can start building in parallel when the existing plant is still running to secure critical supplies.

In principle, a "full repowering" means that one or more gas turbines with downstream heat recovery steam generators replace the old steam generator previously fired with coal or oil. In order to achieve this, various modifications of the steam cycle are necessary, as well as the exchange and retrofit of various components.

For a full repowering, one needs to make sure that the appropriate gas capacities are available. For the final plan, other factors to be considered are the plant capacity, the heat quantities, and levels to be supplied for district heating and/or process steam applications. Also, one needs to consider the space available, and the condition of the power plant. The overall aim is to keep as much of the existing infrastructure as possible.

While it is impressive that by converting a conventional coal power plant to a CCPP CO₂ emissions get reduced by up to 70%, it’s worth mentioning that this is a result not just from the fuel switch, but also from an increase in the power plant’s efficiency from an average of 38% to up to 63%.

A boiler conversion involves a modification of the burner technology and a change of coal or oil to gas. While switching to gas as a fuel does not increase the efficiency of the steam plant, it does reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 50%.

‘Topping’ requires the installation of a small gas turbine, regardless of whether the fuel is switched from coal to gas or not. The thermal energy contained in the flue gas of the ‘topping’ gas turbine is fed directly to the steam generator of the existing plant. This results in a slight improvement in overall plant efficiency.

Boosting requires the installation of an additional – usually medium – gas turbine and a waste heat boiler. In contrast to topping, the heat energy contained in the flue gas of the gas turbine is used with the aid of a heat exchanger to generate high-pressure steam and to preheat the feed water of the existing process. Boosting makes the steam power plant more flexible, while also increasing efficiency and reducing CO₂ emissions.

Parallel repowering utilizes the steam contained in the flue gas of a newly installed large gas turbine with the aid of a heat recovery steam generator for additional feedwater preheating and steam generation in the existing steam power plant process. This conversion also serves to increase the flexibility and efficiency of steam power plants, but to a greater degree than boosting.

Especially for indoor solutions, it’s important to analyze how existing foundations, piping and connections can be reused, while ensuring the new setup will work smoothly and safely.

items.title: Combined heat and power generation
items.description: Discover Siemens Energy's CHP systems delivering high efficiency, reliable power and heat with up to 93% fuel efficiency for sustainable energy use.
items.tags: Gas turbines;;;Power plants;;;Combined heat and power
items.body:
Siemens Energy’s combined heat and power (CHP) plants deliver efficient, sustainable energy. Heat production is responsible for 50% of global energy use and 40% of CO₂ emissions, making it the main source of industrial CO₂ output.

Heat decarbonization, also known as heat transition, is a process for reducing CO₂ emissions from heat production. As a first step, this can be achieved by making fuel usage more efficient. Later, this fossil fuel can be replaced with carbon-free fuel. Alternatively, heat production can also be electrified by using power from renewable energy. Existing heat networks can be transformed fast and at a large scale into cost-effective and flexible low-carbon energy systems.

There are several applications that can help to decarbonize heat networks. Siemens Energy offers tailor-made CHP and Power to Heat (P2H) solutions for the residential, commercial and industrial sectors.

CHP generates electricity and heat from a single fuel source. Traditional heating plants emit varying amounts of CO2 depending on the fuel used. Thus, even a simple fuel switch may reduce CO2 emissions by nearly 50%. Additionally, converting the plant into a GT-powered CHP or a Combined Cycle Power Plant with heat extraction can significantly improve its electrical efficiency. As a result, fuel efficiency can be as high as 90% while using as little fuel as possible.

Find out which gas turbine fits best for your application.

Combined Cycle Power Plants (CCPP) use advanced gas and steam turbines for over 64% efficiency, reduced emissions, and flexible output. The efficient use of fuel results in reduced greenhouse gas emissions. CCPPs can quickly ramp up or down, making them ideal for balancing renewable energy sources.

Learn more about combined cycle power plants.

Clean fuels, such as green hydrogen or biofuels, can drastically lower CO2 emissions and eliminate the need for fossil fuels in gas turbines. This is an effective way to future proof a combined cycle power plant and maximize its life cycle. Find out how much carbon footprint you can reduce by burning green hydrogen in your gas turbine. Calculate your carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction and cost-savings potential on carbon certificates.

Calculate your CO₂ emission reduction potential.

Another decarbonization path is to transform fossil-fired heat generation by switching to sustainably produced biomass in Combined Heat and Power plants. When adding Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS), biomass- or biofuel-based CHP plants can be further transformed into bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), allowing for negative emissions and energy production at the same time.

Learn more about biomass power plant solutions.

For maximum efficiency, it often makes sense to combine different technologies. To make the best choice, there are several factors to consider, such as the required temperature level, dispatchable power needs, green electricity cost, availability of waste heat, and annual heat curve. For instance, if you have a lot of renewable energy, it makes sense to consider Power-to-Heat (P2H).

items.title: Concentrated solar power plants
items.description: Discover Siemens Energy's concentrated solar power solutions: reliable steam turbines, advanced I&C, and thermal storage for round-the-clock renewable power.

faqs.q: What is Concentrated Solar Power (CSP)?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses sunlight to generate electricity. CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate a large area of sunlight onto a small area to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate steam, which drives a steam turbine generator set—the heart of the CSP plant. The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source. Siemens Energy steam turbines are operating in more than 80% of all CSP plants, making the company the market leader in steam turbines for CSP applications. This technology not only contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions but also plays a vital role in the transition to cleaner energy systems.

faqs.q: How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants work?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) is a renewable energy technology that harnesses sunlight to generate electricity. CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate a large area of sunlight onto a small area to produce heat. This heat is then used to generate steam, which drives a steam turbine generator set—the heart of the CSP plant. The steam turbine generator set converts the thermal energy from the steam into mechanical energy, which is then transformed into electrical energy. By efficiently translating solar power into electricity, CSP plants can provide a reliable and sustainable energy source.

faqs.q: How does Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) differ from photovoltaic (PV) solar panels?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and photovoltaic (PV) solar panels are both technologies used to harness solar energy, but they operate on different principles and have distinct characteristics: Energy Conversion Method: CSP: CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate sunlight onto a small area, generating heat that produces steam to drive a steam turbine generator set. This process converts thermal energy into electricity. PV: PV solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using semiconductor materials that generate an electric current when exposed to sunlight. Scale and Application: CSP: Typically used in large-scale power plants, CSP systems are best suited for utility-scale applications where there is ample land and sunlight. They can also incorporate thermal energy storage to provide electricity even when the sun is not shining. PV: PV panels can be deployed in a variety of settings, from small residential rooftops to large solar farms. They are more versatile and can be installed in diverse locations, including urban areas. Efficiency and Performance: CSP: CSP systems can achieve higher efficiencies in converting solar energy to electricity, especially in regions with high direct sunlight. However, they are less effective in cloudy or diffuse light conditions. PV: PV panels are generally more efficient in converting sunlight to electricity under a wider range of conditions, including cloudy weather. Infrastructure and Cost: CSP: CSP plants typically require more extensive infrastructure and higher initial capital costs due to the need for large land areas, mirrors, and thermal storage systems. PV: PV systems have lower installation costs and can be scaled easily, making them more accessible for residential and commercial applications. In summary, while both CSP and PV technologies harness solar energy, they differ in their methods of energy conversion, scale of application, efficiency, and infrastructure requirements.

faqs.q: What are the advantages of CSP plants?
faqs.a: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages that make them an attractive option for renewable energy generation: High Efficiency: CSP systems can achieve higher thermal efficiencies compared to photovoltaic systems, especially in areas with high direct sunlight. This allows for more effective conversion of solar energy into electricity. Energy Storage Capability: Many CSP plants can incorporate thermal energy storage systems, enabling them to store heat for later use. This capability allows for electricity generation even when the sun is not shining, providing a more reliable and consistent power supply. Reduced Greenhouse Gas Emissions: By utilizing solar energy, CSP plants significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to fossil fuel-based power generation, contributing to a cleaner environment and helping combat climate change. Scalability: CSP plants can be built at various scales, from small installations to large utility-scale facilities, making them adaptable to different energy needs and geographical locations. Job Creation: The construction and operation of CSP plants create jobs in engineering, manufacturing, and maintenance, contributing to local economies and promoting sustainable development. Complementary to Other Energy Sources: CSP can be integrated with other renewable energy sources and traditional power plants, providing a hybrid approach that enhances overall energy reliability and stability. Long Operational Life: CSP plants typically have long operational lifespans, often exceeding 25 years, which allows for sustained energy production and return on investment over time. These advantages position CSP plants as a viable and effective solution for meeting growing energy demands while promoting sustainability and reducing environmental impact.

faqs.q: What are the main challenges or disadvantages of CSP?
faqs.a: While Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants offer several advantages, they also face some challenges and disadvantages: High Initial Costs: CSP plants typically require significant capital investment for construction and infrastructure, which can be a barrier to development compared to other renewable energy technologies. Land Use Requirements: CSP systems require large areas of land to accommodate mirrors or heliostats, which can lead to land use conflicts, especially in densely populated or ecologically sensitive areas. Dependence on Direct Sunlight: CSP technology is most effective in regions with high direct sunlight and can be less efficient in areas with cloudy or diffuse light conditions. This limits the geographical applicability of CSP plants. Complexity of Technology: The technology involved in CSP systems, including thermal storage and heat transfer fluids, can be complex and may require specialized knowledge for operation and maintenance. Intermittency: Although CSP plants can store thermal energy, they still rely on sunlight for operation. This intermittency can pose challenges for grid integration and reliability, particularly during periods of low solar availability. Environmental Impact: The construction and operation of CSP plants can have environmental impacts, including habitat disruption and changes to local ecosystems, which need to be carefully managed. These challenges highlight the need for careful planning, investment, and technological innovation to maximize the potential of CSP as a sustainable energy solution.

faqs.q: How much electricity can a typical CSP plant generate?
faqs.a: A typical Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plant can generate a range of electricity depending on its size, technology, and location. Most CSP plants have capacities ranging from 10 megawatts (MW) to over 100 MW. For example, a 100 MW CSP plant can produce approximately 300,000 to 400,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity annually, depending on factors such as solar irradiance, operational efficiency, and the inclusion of thermal energy storage. In optimal conditions, larger CSP plants can achieve even higher outputs, contributing significantly to the energy grid and providing a reliable source of renewable energy. The actual generation will vary based on local climate conditions and the specific design of the CSP system.

faqs.q: How does thermal energy storage work in CSP plants?
faqs.a: Thermal energy storage (TES) in Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants allows for the capture and storage of heat generated during sunlight hours, enabling electricity generation even when the sun is not shining. The process typically involves the following steps: Heat Collection: During the day, CSP systems use mirrors or heliostats to concentrate sunlight onto a receiver, where it heats a heat transfer fluid (HTF), commonly molten salt or water. Heat Transfer: The heated HTF is then circulated to a thermal energy storage system, where it transfers its heat to a storage medium. In many CSP plants, molten salt is used due to its high heat capacity and ability to remain in a liquid state at elevated temperatures. Storage: The thermal energy is stored in the form of sensible heat within the molten salt or other storage mediums. This allows the system to retain heat for several hours or even days, depending on the design and capacity of the storage system. Energy Release: When electricity demand increases or during periods of low sunlight, the stored thermal energy is released. The HTF is circulated back to the steam generator, where it transfers heat to water, producing steam. Electricity Generation: The steam drives a steam turbine generator set, converting the thermal energy back into electricity. This process allows CSP plants to provide a continuous and reliable power supply, even during nighttime or cloudy conditions. By incorporating thermal energy storage, CSP plants enhance their operational flexibility and reliability, making them a valuable component of the renewable energy landscape.

faqs.q: Why is concentrated solar power similar to a power plant that uses fossil fuels?
faqs.a: CSP plants are renewable and produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions during operation, while fossil fuel plants contribute to carbon emissions and environmental pollution. Despite this distinction, from a technical perspective, both power plant types share several similarities: Thermal Energy Generation: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants generate electricity by producing steam. In CSP plants, sunlight is concentrated to heat a fluid, creating steam, while fossil fuel plants burn coal, natural gas, or oil to produce heat that generates steam. Steam Turbine Technology: Both types of power plants utilize steam turbines to convert thermal energy into mechanical energy. The steam produced in both systems drives a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity. Heat Transfer Systems: Both CSP and fossil fuel plants rely on heat transfer systems to move thermal energy. In CSP, heat transfer fluids (like molten salt) are used, while fossil fuel plants typically use water or steam as the heat transfer medium. Infrastructure and Operation: The operational infrastructure, including boilers, turbines, and generators, is conceptually similar in both CSP and fossil fuel plants. Both require significant engineering and maintenance to ensure efficient operation. Grid Integration: Both CSP and fossil fuel power plants are integrated into the electrical grid, providing power to meet demand. They can both contribute to base-load or peak-load generation, depending on the design and operational strategy. These technical similarities highlight how CSP can serve as a cleaner alternative to traditional fossil fuel power generation while still utilizing established technologies for electricity production.

faqs.q: What types of CSP technologies does Siemens Energy support?
faqs.a: There are three different types of Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants: Solar Tower Technology: In this design, heliostats bundle sunlight onto the top of a high tower,. Parabolic Trough: This technology uses parabolic mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a pipeline located in the middle of the mirrors, heating a fluid that produces steam. Fresnel Technology: This type is becoming less common and is hardly used anymore. Siemens Energy has proven experience with all three types of CSP technologies. Among these, the parabolic trough is the most often built type to date, known for its efficiency and reliability in harnessing solar energy. Our expertise across these technologies enables us to provide comprehensive solutions and support for CSP projects, ensuring optimal performance and integration into the energy grid.

faqs.q: How do Siemens Energy steam turbines optimize CSP plant performance?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy steam turbines play a crucial role in optimizing the performance of Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants. These turbines are specifically designed to handle the unique operational demands of CSP systems, which often require managing daily starts and stops due to varying sunlight conditions. As a result, Siemens Energy steam turbines must be designed in a very robust way to ensure reliability and efficiency during these frequent operational changes. With extensive experience in the field, Siemens Energy has been a pioneer in CSP technology, having installed the first steam turbine in a CSP plant as early as the 1980s. This long history has provided valuable insights into the performance requirements and challenges of CSP applications. Our steam turbines are engineered to deliver high efficiency, quick response times, and durability, enabling CSP plants to maximize energy output while minimizing downtime. By integrating advanced technologies and optimizing turbine design, Siemens Energy steam turbines enhance the overall efficiency and reliability of CSP plants, contributing to a more sustainable and effective renewable energy solution.

items.body:
Concentrated solar thermal power is worldwide becoming a more and more important source for power generation. The reasons for this are obvious: The sun is an inexhaustible source for power production. And it is not only a free fuel source but also a complete emissions-free source. Steam turbine generator sets convert solar energy into electricity. Instrumentation and controlls help to make optimal use of every single sun beam. As a market leader in the field, Siemens Energy equipped more than 70 concetrated solar power (CSP) plants all over the world.

Dubai’s new CSP plant is designed to collect heat from the sun and store it in molten salt or convert it directly into electricity via a steam generator set – an ideal solution for providing round-the-clock renewable electricity in unpredictable conditions. Noor Energy 1, the 950 MW Hybrid Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) and PV plant, is the 4th phase of the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Plant and the largest single -site CSP and single hybrid solar power project in the world.

Since the solar boom of the eighties in USA, solar thermal energy has been a proven technology. The most common type of plant is the parabolic trough collector, but alternative technologies are rapidly coming to the fore, such as Linear Fresnel collector plants with flat mirrors and central tower plants with slightly curved mirrors or heliostats.

The basic principle is the same for all three plant technologies: Mirrors concentrate the incident solar radiation onto a receiver where it is converted into heat that is used to produce steam to drive a steam turbine. Heat storage systems like molten salt tanks provide for power supply even during unfavorable weather conditions or at night. They significantly increase the number of full-load operation hours with optimal steam turbine efficiency.

With our broad steam turbine portfolio, we offer a range of turbines for different types of solar plants and all power outputs. The turbine technology fits all three common concentrated solar power concepts. We were the first steam turbine supplier to re-enter the CSP market in the 21st century, pioneering commercial solutions in the US and Spain. Today, we are the world market leader in steam turbines for CSP plants, and have more than 20 years of experience with steam turbines for daily cycling.

Parabolic systems use trough-shaped mirrors to focus sunlight onto an absorber tube (receiver) placed in the trough’s focal line. The troughs are designed to track the sun along one axis, predominantly north-south. The receivers contain a heat transfer fluid (e.g. synthetic thermal oil, molten salt) which is heated by the focused sunlight. It is circulated in these tubes and pumped through heat exchangers to produce steam.

The parabolic trough technology is currently the best proven and most used technology, even though the live steam parameters are lower than in solar power tower plants.

A circular array of flat heliostats (suntracking mirrors) concentrates sunlight on to a central receiver at the top of a tower. A heat transfer medium (water/steam, molten salt or air) in the receiver absorbs the thermal energy and transfers it into the steam cycle to generate superheated steam for the turbine.

The advantage over the parabolic trough or Fresnel collector concept is that the sunlight on the central receiver is focused to a smaller area, and the heat transfer medium does not have to be piped around the large solar field. This means that higher working fluid temperatures in the receiver (up to 1000°C) and better steam parameters are feasible, even supercritical steam is expected.

The number of concentrated solar power plants has increased tremendously in the past ten years. Today we see many different regimes of operations, each of which poses a different challenge to power generation equipment. The design of each steam turbine is adapted to these challenges.

As market leader in industrial steam turbines, we command a comprehensive product portfolio for solar thermal plants, covering the full range from 1.5 MW to more than 250 MW.

CSP plants require steam turbines which are optimized for their complex and challenging cycle conditions. Bearing in mind that efficiency and total cost of ownership are key to any investment decision, we incorporate operational experience into extensive R&D and engineering activities to adapt the turbines to the specific requirements of the CSP technology.

Day and night cycle often requires a large number of starts and fast daily startup capabilities from CSP steam turbines. When focusing on annual power production, the short start-up times of the turbines are of great benefit to the CSP plant owner. Daily cycling and temperature variations require special attention.

Reheat solutions improve efficiency and reduce problems with erosion/corrosion and moisture in the LP turbine. Our steam turbines meet all customer requirements for economic installation and operation and provide excellent flexibility for all cycling conditions. The turbines are suitable for higher steam parameters and can be operated in non-reheat, single reheat and double reheat cycles.

Our steam turbines are tailored to the customer requirements and shipped assembled for easy installation at site. This reduces time and manpower in the installation phase. All steam turbines are available with axial or radial exhaust and suitable for air- and water-cooled plants.

We provide optimal instrumentation and controls (I&C) design for CSP & Hybrid-PV plants for achieving the full dispatchability of solar energy power plants. With start-up and shut-down 365 days a year, high demands are placed on your plant even on the sunniest of days. Thanks to our I&C’s integration expertise in steam turbine controls, balance-of-plant, and solar fields the plant’s performance is optimized and long-term reliability is maintained.

Flexible and optimized plant operation with minimized operator interactions thanks to fast, reliable and reproducible fully automatic “Golden button” unit startup.

items.title: Grid resilience
items.description: Discover grid resilience products and solutions focused on building a robust, reliable, and automated grid to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.

faqs.q: What is grid resilience?
faqs.a: An increasing system complexity demands for investments into grid infrastructure that stabilize the grid and ensure uninterrupted energy supply, even under adverse conditions. Grid resilience ensures stability, reliability and availability of the grid, reduces losses and improves system efficiency.

faqs.q: What is grid stability?
faqs.a: Grid stability is what keeps the challenges to power systems, such as the spikes or lulls in demand, power line, or even generator failure, in check. Since power is produced on demand, it's critical to ensure that the power system frequency and voltage remain within normal ranges. Maintaining this balance is necessary to keep the power grid stable and efficient.

faqs.q: What is the difference between grid resilience and grid reliability?
faqs.a: Grid resilience is the ability of the power grid to prepare for, respond to, and recover from disruptive events, such as natural disasters, or equipment failures. Focus is the grid’s adaptability and robustness in the face of unexpected challenges, ensuring that it can bounce back quickly and maintain service continuity. Grid reliability refers to the ability of the power system to consistently deliver electricity to consumers without interruption. It encompasses the performance of the grid in terms of its capacity to meet demand and the frequency and duration of outages. With our grid resilience offerings, we ensure efficient power grid operations through reliability, availability and stability – anywhere, anytime.

faqs.q: How to increase grid resilience?
faqs.a: At Siemens Energy Grid Technologies, we offer a broad portfolio of innovative transmission products, systems, solutions, and services to support customers on their energy transition journeys towards more resilient grids. With our offerings, we enhance grid stability by using technologies to manage renewable energy intermittency, ensuring a steady power supply, focus on modernizing aging infrastructure to improve grid reliability and efficiency, and ensure consistent power availability through our services. Additionally, we optimize electricity flow to reduce losses, and implement strategies for sustainability and longevity, minimizing environmental impact while maximizing reliability.

items.body:
To power the energy transition, we need a robust and reliable grid. Siemens Energy focus is on enhancing and automating the grid, ensuring it's equipped to handle the demands of tomorrow. The high-voltage solutions, products and services enable efficient, loss-minimal transportation of renewable energy to global cities and hubs. Leveraging cutting-edge digital technologies, we optimize grid performance, even when dealing with large volumes of fluctuating energy and ultra-short-term renewable energy storage.

The power sector is undergoing a transformative period marked by rapid changes and innovations. Key drivers of this transformation include the push for decarbonization, the rise of electrification, and the liberalization of energy markets. As renewable energy sources like solar and wind become more prevalent, they introduce variability and reduce the inertia of traditional power systems, which rely on rotating masses.

This shift presents unique challenges in maintaining grid stability, particularly in terms of voltage, frequency, and load management. Additionally, the growing demand for electricity and the need for enhanced interconnections between power systems add to the complexity. Ensuring grid resiliency is crucial for meeting these challenges, providing a stable and reliable power supply, and facilitating the transition to a sustainable energy future.

Siemens Energy enhances a resilient grid through innovative solutions, advanced technologies, and smart grid integration, ensuring a reliable and sustainable energy future.

The share of electric power produced from renewable energy sources is growing worldwide. FACTS are the perfect solution for increasing the reliability of AC grids, ensuring stability, and boosting transmission efficiency.

Siemens Energy transformers are deployed across a wide range of applications—from renewable energy and industrial operations to urban infrastructure and critical facilities. Engineered for performance, reliability, and sustainability, they support the evolving needs of modern power systems and the global energy transition.

HVDC is ideal for bridging the distances between large-scale renewable power generating installations such as offshore wind farms and the load centers they serve.

Integrating renewable energy sources is key to meeting society’s energy needs. We supply the entire range of products and services required for turnkey solutions that efficiently harness the power of offshore renewables and deliver energy to the end consumer.

Energy storage is critical to decarbonizing the power system and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Our battery energy storage systems consist of one or more batteries and can be used to balance the electric grid, provide backup power, and improve grid stability.

High-voltage transmission assets are a critical part to supply high quality energy to our society. With our offerings, we implement strategies to improve the efficiency and longevity of electrical grids, while minimizing environmental impact and maximizing reliability.

As the energy landscape shifts towards renewables and grid modernization, advanced substation technologies help operators maintain grid reliability, protect infrastructure, adapt to changing demands, and integrate renewable energy with flexibility.

The grid of the future needs digital solutions to make today’s utilization more efficient, more flexible and to address evolving complexities. Noedra is Siemens Energy’s power grids digital framework, bringing together intelligent solutions into one connected ecosystem.

faqs.q: What is Power-to-X and how does it work?
faqs.a: Power-to-X as the key technology in sector coupling allows us to transform and save energy from renewable resources in a chemical form for long-term storage and use in mobility or industry.

faqs.q: What are the main applications of Power-to-X?
faqs.a: Power-to-X enables the production of various types of synthetic fuels like eKerosene, eMethanol, eAmmonia and eGasoline from green hydrogen and a low-emission carbon source. These e-Fuels can help decarbonize the aviation, shipping, fertilizer and transportation industry.

faqs.q: How efficient is Power-to-X technology?
faqs.a: One key lever for efficient Power-to-X technology is high availability of renewable energy in regions with abundant wind or sun.

faqs.q: How does Power-to-X compare to traditional energy sources in terms of efficiency?
faqs.a: Power-to-X uses renewable energy to produce hydrogen or fuel molecules. This is less efficient than directly using electricity. But it provides a chance to decarbonize industries that cannot be electrified, like shipping, aviation, steel production, etc.

faqs.q: What are the main challenges in implementing Power-to-X technologies?
faqs.a: Power-to-X plants need a high availability of renewable energy and for the synthesis of e-Fuels a Carbon source is needed. Although investment costs for Power-to-X will decrease during the next years according to technology development, regulation and political support are needed to push the introduction of e-Fuels.

faqs.q: What are the environmental benefits of using Power-to-X?
faqs.a: Power-to-X enables the production of various types of synthetic fuels like eKerosene, eMethanol, eAmmonia and eGasoline from green hydrogen and a low-emission carbon source. These e-Fuels can help decarbonize the aviation, shipping, fertilizer and transportation industry.

faqs.q: How does Power-to-X contribute to the decarbonization of the energy sector?
faqs.a: Sector coupling is the energetic link of sectors like power, energy, mobility, industry or building. It acts as a link between renewable energy sources (wind, solar, water...) and consumers. Power-to-X as the key technology in sector coupling allows us to transform and save energy from renewable resources in a chemical form for long-term storage and use.

faqs.q: How can Siemens Energy support my project with Power-to-X solutions?
faqs.a: Siemens Energy is the only manufacturer of Power-to-X solutions with the portfolio, experience and knowledge of power generation, electrolysis and grid connection. We use our expertise and our tools for system design and simulation to determine optimum technical and economic solutions for you. We offer all project steps starting from feasibility studies, FEED studies, project management and service.

Sector coupling is the energetic link of sectors like power, energy, mobility, industry or building. It acts as a link between renewable energy sources (wind, solar, water...) and consumers.

Power-to-X as the key technology in sector coupling allows us to transform and save energy from renewable resources in a chemical form for long-term storage and use, with green hydrogen and its derivatives as the core component.

Discover how Power-to-X technology is transforming the energy landscape, harmonizing diverse sectors and paving the way for a sustainable future. Watch the video!

Power-to-X (PtX) and hybrid solutions are always a subset of the energy landscape shown in the image. In PtX applications, hydrogen is converted into molecules along the energy landscape via a synthesis process, but no re-electrification takes place.

The provision of renewable energy in the form of green hydrogen and its derivatives opens up new business areas and offers additional benefits. With our technical know-how and additional services, we provide you with optimal Power-to-X solutions.

Green hydrogen can be used to produce various types of synthetic fuels like eKerosene, eMethanol, eAmmonia and eGasoline, which support the decarbonization of the aviation, shipping, fertilizer and transportation industry. In energy-intensive industries like steel production, it can replace gray hydrogen and other substances directly through green hydrogen production.

In the future, non-fossil e-Methanol will see vast new application fields. This paper focuses on the green hydrogen path, which uses renewable electricity:

Find out more about the economic feasibility, key markets and applications of e-Ammonia around the world in connection with Power-to-X:

The generation of renewable energies is one side of the coin. How can you ensure a reliable and constantly available energy supply for your system in a cost-effective way? Discover the right solution for your project!

Grid connected Power-to-X projects provide stable power-supply, however, they are facing challenges regarding grid code requirements as well as regulatory boundary conditions. We take care of seamless connection and interaction with the grid, dispatch control according to regulatory requirements (e.g. hourly correlation) as well as digital certification of your product in terms of CO₂ footprint.

Siemens Energy is the only manufacturer of Power-to-X solutions with the portfolio, experience and knowledge of power generation and grid connection. We use our expertise and our tolls for system design and simulation to determine optimum technical and economic solutions for you. As an additional benefit, electrolysis can be used as a fast energy balancing unit and its end products as energy storage.

Off-Grid Power-to-X projects provide advantages regarding compliance with regulatory requirements due to inherent geographic and timely correlation. In addition, grid utilization charges can be avoided. The biggest challenge for off-grid or weak-grid projects lies in designing the grid forming and stabilizing equipment in close connection with an integrated control system. Siemens Energy has acquired significant experience in modelling complex island grids from renewables to the electrolyzers and other downstream consumers, which is the basis for simulation and optimization of essential grid stabilizing systems such as batteries, synchronous condensers or static converters.

Our comprehensive services offer you a risk reduction in implementation and overall availability of the plant. They help you to increase your benefits and your return on investment.

Our feasibility studies develop tailored, economic solutions for sustainability, reducing carbon footprint. With our proven Energy System Design approach, we create optimal solutions for complex energy systems.

Pre-FEED studies offer valuable insights into project feasibility, costs, and benefits. Early risk and opportunity identification enables informed decision-making and maximizes investment profitability.

FEEDs provide you with a clear and comprehensive insight into your project's requirements and costs, empowering you to make informed decisions and maximize your investment profitability.

items.title: Zero Emission Hydrogen Turbine Center
items.description: Discover the Zero Emission Hydrogen Turbine Center and how hydrogen, renewables, and storage support flexible, low-carbon power systems.
items.body:
The next decades are expected to be among the most transformative the energy sector has ever seen when the world is moving away from fossil fuels. As part of this transformation we expanded our own gas turbine test facility in the town of Finspång, Sweden, to become a model of the future energy system.

Together with international partners within the research project Zero Emission Hydrogen Turbine Center (ZEHTC) we set up a demonstration plant to showcase a flexible and sustainable energy system connecting gas turbines with hydrogen, renewable energy and energy storage. This provided valuable insights to be able to accelerate into a decarbonized energy future.

Onsite hydrogen production from renewables and excess electricity

Hydrogen enabling decarbonization of gas turbine operation

Platform for sharing know-how on flexible energy systems and hydrogen solutions

Enabling extended testing toward 100 percent hydrogen capability

The demonstrator plant provides valuable insights to be able to accelerate into a decarbonized energy future.

Read more about the project and all the partners on our partner website

The test center opens up multiple possibilities: Excess energy from gas turbine tests and electricity from solar panels is used to produce hydrogen in an electrolyzer. The energy is stored as compressed hydrogen and in batteries.

This way a closed loop plant is created, producing its own hydrogen for our continued research and development to optimize the use of hydrogen in gas turbines. All this also while supporting our goal to be able to run our gas turbines on 100% hydrogen by 2030.

Click on the labels to learn more about the components of the solution

So, what is the role of gas turbines in a sustainable energy system?

Gas turbines have proven to be very effective in balancing intermittent renewable energy production due to their flexibility and short ramp-up times. According to the International Energy Agency, gas turbines will play an important role in providing flexibility in the electrical grid in a Sustainable Development Scenario.

As of today, the gas turbines we're testing in our new Zero Emission Hydrogen Turbine Center are ready to burn up to 75% of hydrogen in the fuel mix. And step by step we aim to reach 100% by 2030.

items.h1: Industrial AI: Strategies for industrial transformation
items.description: Siemens Energy is pioneering the next wave of Industrial AI focusing on autonomous, context-aware agents capable of executing complex tasks and workflows.

faqs.q: What is Industrial AI?
faqs.a: Industrial AI refers to the application of artificial intelligence technologies in industrial environments to optimize processes, enhance productivity, and enable data-driven decision-making. It combines machine learning, automation, and domain expertise to solve complex operational challenges.

faqs.q: What are the main challenges in implementing Industrial AI?
faqs.a: Key challenges include data quality and availability, integration with legacy systems, workforce readiness, and cybersecurity. Successful implementation requires a clear strategy, cross-functional collaboration, and scalable infrastructure.

faqs.q: Can Industrial AI help reduce operational costs?
faqs.a: Yes, Industrial AI can significantly reduce operational costs by automating repetitive tasks, optimizing resource usage, predicting equipment failures, and improving supply chain efficiency. These improvements lead to measurable savings and increased profitability.

faqs.q: Is Industrial AI scalable across different energy sectors?
faqs.a: Industrial AI is highly scalable and adaptable across various energy sectors, including power generation, transmission, distribution, and renewable energy. Its modular design allows tailored solutions for diverse operational needs.

faqs.q: How does Industrial AI contribute to sustainability?
faqs.a: Industrial AI supports sustainability by optimizing energy consumption, reducing waste, and enabling predictive maintenance. It helps industries lower their carbon footprint and transition toward more efficient, eco-friendly operations.

faqs.q: How does Industrial AI improve energy grid reliability?
faqs.a: Industrial AI enhances energy grid reliability through predictive analytics, real-time monitoring, and automated fault detection. It helps balance supply and demand, prevent outages, and optimize grid performance for stable energy delivery.

faqs.q: How is AI shaping the future of industrial automation?
faqs.a: AI is transforming industrial automation by enabling intelligent systems that learn, adapt, and make decisions in real time. From autonomous robots to smart factories, AI drives innovation, flexibility, and responsiveness in industrial operations.

faqs.q: Can Industrial AI help reduce operational costs?
faqs.a: Industrial AI can significantly reduce operational costs by automating repetitive tasks, optimizing resource usage, predicting equipment failures, and improving supply chain efficiency. These improvements lead to measurable savings and increased profitability.

faqs.q: What kind of data is required for Industrial AI applications?
faqs.a: Industrial AI relies on structured and unstructured data from sensors, machines, enterprise systems, and historical records. High-quality data is essential for accurate predictions, automation, and continuous learning.

faqs.q: What is the outlook for Industrial AI in the energy landscape?
faqs.a: The future of Industrial AI in the energy sector is promising, with growing adoption of intelligent systems for grid management, renewable integration, asset management and modernization of legacy infrastructure as well as operational optimization. It plays a key role in driving digital transformation and energy transition.

items.body:
The future of the energy sector is being reshaped by Industrial Artificial Intelligence (Industrial AI). As energy systems become increasingly interconnected and complex, the demand for faster, smarter decision-making grows. Industrial AI empowers companies to navigate this complexity, optimize operations, and accelerate business growth in a rapidly evolving energy landscape.

Siemens Energy is pioneering the next wave of Industrial AI focusing on autonomous, context-aware agents capable of executing complex tasks and workflows.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed everyday life - from smartphone face recognition to personalized online experiences. Yet, its application in industrial sectors - known as Industrial AI - promises to revolutionize manufacturing, energy, mining, logistics, and more, delivering profound societal and economic impact at scale.

In manufacturing and engineering, Siemens Energy applies AI to enhance the full product lifecycle, from design to operation. This includes AI‑supported design generation, 3D product synthesis, and simulation to accelerate development and improve product performance. AI is also used for intelligent requirement management, product and component optimization, smart quality control, and engineering support copilots, enabling higher quality, efficiency, and faster time‑to‑market.

Despite its promise, Industrial AI adoption faces significant hurdles:

Lack of business-aligned transformation roadmaps

Many organizations follow a technology maturity model (e.g., from descriptive to prescriptive analytics) that doesn’t align with urgent business needs, causing delays in deploying impactful AI solutions. Improved communication and alignment between IT and operations is essential.

Requirement for multi-disciplinary expertise

Successful Industrial AI demands collaboration among domain experts, AI specialists, and IT infrastructure teams. Industrial environments pose challenges such as data heterogeneity, safety requirements, and system robustness, complicating AI deployment.

Complexity in mapping business needs with technical solutions

Industrial processes are complex and dynamic, with variable demand and unpredictable equipment failures. Aligning these nuanced business requirements with a vast, evolving portfolio of AI technologies requires strong leadership and proficiency.

AI drives power demand – and vice versa. According to the International Energy Agency, global electricity consumption by data centers is projected to more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030– a quantity roughly equivalent to Japan’s annual electricity consumption today. Power availability has become a top priority in decisions about data center locations.

The paradox: Compute-intensive AI will be one of the fastest-growing drivers of electricity demand while AI is essential for making power systems themselves more resilient, efficient, and flexible. This dual role positions Industrial AI not as a peripheral technology, but as a structural enabler of future energy operations.

The energy industry needs to carefully embed AI into systems that drive or influence operational decisions. Failures can have severe financial, safety, or environmental consequences. Operators must be able to trace, audit, and verify every decision. Human oversight remains essential. In practice, this means architects need to design Industrial AI systems so that: decisions are explainable and verifiable, Industrial AI supports existing safety and control frameworks, data security is ensured, human operators retain final authority, systems are seamlessly integrated with deterministic control logic, and cybersecurity is embedded at every layer.

Industrial AI is revolutionizing energy operations through diverse, high-impact applications:

Siemens Energy is pioneering the next wave of Industrial AI: Agentic AI.

Moving beyond traditional Generative AI, Agentic AI focuses on autonomous, context-aware agents capable of executing complex tasks and workflows.

By harnessing Agentic AI, Siemens Energy helps customers unlock new levels of operational efficiency and business growth, while advancing a sustainable energy future.

faqs.q: What is heat decarbonization?
faqs.a: Heat decarbonization means reducing or removing carbon dioxide emissions from heat production and use. This can be achieved by using fuel in more efficient ways, e.g. by utilizing it for captive power generation (waste heat recovery). Carbon-free fuels could replace fossil fuel. Alternatively, you can electrify heat production by using power from renewable energy.

faqs.q: What are the main benefits of decarbonizing process steam?
faqs.a: Decarbonizing process steam significantly reduces greenhouse gas emissions, leading to a lower carbon footprint for industries. Additionally, it offers long-term energy cost savings and helps ensure compliance with regulatory standards aimed at promoting sustainability.

faqs.q: What challenges do industries face when implementing waste heat recovery?
faqs.a: Industries often encounter economic barriers related to initial investments and may struggle with integrating new technologies into existing systems without disrupting operations.

faqs.q: Can hydrogen be used in existing heating systems?
faqs.a: Yes, hydrogen can replace natural gas in many uses. For example the so-called green steel could be produced by replaing fossil fuels with hydrogen. However, changes may be needed based on the heating system's needs.

faqs.q: What is waste heat recovery?
faqs.a: Waste heat recovery captures and reuses the heat generated by industrial processes that would otherwise get lost. This recovered heat can be used in other processes. It can also generate electricity. This helps improve energy efficiency and lowers overall energy costs.

items.body:
Decarbonizing heat, particularly in industrial settings and district heating systems, is critical. Industrial heat represents about 29% of global energy consumption; it is responsible for 15% of greenhouse gas emissions. Industries are under pressure to lower their carbon dioxide footprints. Additionally, district heating systems present unique challenges in this transition, necessitating innovative solutions to achieve effective decarbonization.

We, as Siemens Energy, have a comprehensive approach, which includes collaboration with industry partners and a commitment to sustainability. That positions us as a leader in driving the energy transition and achieving sustainable, low-carbon energy systems reducing environmental impact.

Processes in many industrial sectors often require extremely high temperatures, traditionally achieved using fossil fuels, making the transition to low-carbon alternatives technically challenging. Additionally, some processes inherently produce CO₂, requiring solutions such as carbon capture and storage.

District heating providers have systems that work at high temperatures. This makes it hard and expensive to add low-temperature and renewable heat sources.

Many technologies are leading the way in reducing carbon emissions from heat to cover energy demand. You can divide these into two main types. One type focuses on cutting CO₂ emissions during heat production. The other type aims to improve energy efficiency, especially by using waste or unused heat.

Industrial heat decarbonization relies on a mix of technologies, often tailored to the temperature range and specific process needs.

Utilizing organic materials as fuel can significantly lower carbon emissions. Biomass can replace burning fossil fuels in various applications, providing a renewable source of energy.

Green hydrogen is a clean fuel option. These applications usually depend on natural gas. This technology is gaining traction as industries seek to electrify their processes.

Our Turbo Heaters provide high-temperature process heat at an industrial scale without burning fossil fuels. When powered by green electricity, they operate with zero CO₂ emissions.

By integrating waste heat recovery into district heating systems, industries can provide sustainable heating solutions to communities while reducing overall emissions.

Often heat is unused because of dust loading, intermittend processes or accessibility. To manage these challenges, different technologies exist to transfer heat to power. One example is the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) technology, which allows for the efficient conversion of low-temperature heat into electricity. This process is known as organic rankine cycle waste heat recovery. This process greatly improves energy efficiency.

Mechanical Vapor Recompression (MVR) cycles use integrally geared compressors. They offer a different way to recover waste heat temperature levels from approximately 60°C (i.e. mid-temperature levels). This process can create hot water e.g. for district heating, or steam at different pressure levels for either district heating or industrial applications.

Steam compression is a sustainable method of generating useable steam from waste steam. This technology can achieve the steam temperatures and pressures required by many processes.

By using both a gas turbine and a steam turbine, combined cycle power plants can generate more electricity from the same amount of fuel compared to a simple cycle gas plant, because it combines two thermodynamic cycles: the Brayton cycle (gas turbine) and the Rankine cycle (steam turbine).

Reducing carbon emissions from industrial heat is not only vital for protecting our environment—it also opens the door to innovation and leadership in sustainable practices. By adopting tailored low-carbon technologies, industries can significantly cut their carbon footprints while enhancing operational efficiency.

Looking ahead, collaboration and investment from industry leaders are crucial to accelerate this transition. Get involved in decarbonization efforts today—your engagement can help shape a cleaner, more resilient future.

items.h1: Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) solutions for low-grade heat recovery
items.description: Recover low and medium temperature heat with these ORC solutions. Improve efficiency, reduce emissions, and generate power from waste heat or geothermal sources

faqs.q: What is an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) system?
faqs.a: An Organic Rankine Cycle uses an organic fluid with a low boiling point instead of water/steam to convert low- to medium-temperature heat (typically 80 - 400°C) into electricity in a closed loop.

faqs.q: How does ORC differ from a traditional steam turbine?
faqs.a: ORC handles lower-temperature heat sources that steam turbines cannot efficiently use, employing organic fluids for vaporization at reduced pressures; steam turbines require higher temperatures (>400°C) and water/steam.

faqs.q: What are typical ORC efficiency levels?
faqs.a: ORC systems achieve 5–20% thermal efficiency depending on heat source temperature, lower than steam turbines (>40%) but valuable for recovering otherwise wasted low-grade heat.

faqs.q: What are common ORC applications?
faqs.a: ORC excels in waste heat recovery (industrial exhaust, cement/steel plants), geothermal power, biomass, solar thermal, and CHP/district heating.

faqs.q: Can ORC systems operate without water?
faqs.a: Yes, many ORC designs, including Siemens Energy's geothermal modules, are water-free using air cooling or dry fluids, ideal for water-scarce sites.

faqs.q: What industries use ORC for waste heat recovery?
faqs.a: Energy-intensive sectors like cement (up to 30% plant power), steel, glass, chemicals, and refineries recover flue gas/pre-heater heat to generate captive power and cut emissions.

faqs.q: What temperature range suits ORC technology?
faqs.a: ORC works best for low- to medium-grade heat: 80–400°C for waste heat/geothermal; Siemens small ORC handles 140–300°C circuits efficiently.

faqs.q: What are ORC benefits for decarbonization?
faqs.a: ORC recovers stranded heat, reducing fuel use/emissions by 10–30% in plants, supporting net-zero goals without process changes; enables CHP for district heating.

faqs.q: How does Siemens Energy support ORC projects?
faqs.a: From feasibility studies and engineering to digital controls (SPPA-T3000), installation, and lifecycle services for modernization/LTO, ensuring high availability.

items.body:
Many industrial processes and geothermal reservoirs release valuable low- to medium-temperature heat that conventional steam cycles cannot use efficiently. Siemens Energy Organic Rankine Cycle solutions convert that heat into electricity in a closed loop, helping you recover stranded energy, reduce emissions, and improve overall efficiency with a compact, water-lean system.

The Organic Rankine Cycle is a proven technology for generating electricity from heat sources that are too cool for conventional steam cycles. By using an organic working fluid with a low boiling point, ORC systems make low-grade heat economically usable.

ORC systems are well suited for waste heat recovery, geothermal applications, and sites where compact, efficient, and water-lean power generation is needed. They help customers reduce fuel waste, strengthen energy resilience, and improve plant economics.

Decarbonizing heat, particularly in industrial settings and district heating systems, is critical. Industrial heat represents about 29% of global energy consumption; it is responsible for 15% of greenhouse gas emissions. Industries are under pressure to lower their carbon dioxide footprints, necessitating innovative solutions to achieve effective decarbonization

The Organic Rankine Cycle system captures low to medium temperature heat from waste streams or geothermal sources to vaporize an organic working fluid in heat exchangers which are arranged in series; the high‑pressure vapor expands through a turbine to drive a generator. The vapor is then condensed and pumped back to the heat exchangers, forming a closed loop that efficiently converts heat into electricity where conventional steam cycles aren’t able.

The Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) converts low‑ to medium‑temperature heat into electricity by vaporizing an organic fluid to drive a turbine generator in a closed, efficient loop where steam cycles are ineffective.

Heat from your source (e.g. flue gases from industrial processes, exhaust of gas turbine or geothermal water) is utilized in the heat exchangers to pre-heat, vaporize and super-heat (if applicable) the ORC fluid.

The superheated organic vapor expands through the ORC turbine to produce shaft power.

The turbine drives the generator to deliver electricity to your plant. A recuperator boosts cycle efficiency, and a water condenser can supply useful heat for CHP/district heating.

No water usage, low emissions and limited noise pollution support a better climate.

State of the art technology, providing remote and unmanned operations, ready for a new era.

Unattended operation possible with low demand on repair and maintenance.

Recuperated and non-recuperated cycle possible

Highly efficient ORC-Turbine based on proven Siemens Energy steam turbine portfolio with a wide operation range from 10 up to 100%. Good part Ioad efficiency.

Main design principle of ORC systems is a closed cycle to avoid any leakages into the atmosphere, e.g. by applying mechanical seals of rotating shafts.

With more than 100 years of experience in the steam turbine business, steam turbines are at the very heart of who we are. Siemens Energy ORC turbines carry the same proven DNA, engineered with the expertise, reliability, and innovation built over a century. Each ORC solution we offer is deeply rooted in our heritage and experience, delivering performance you can trust.

Our ORC Turbine Technology is a modern, high efficiency variant engineered to convert low to medium temperature heat into electricity for both industrial and geothermal applications. Built on proven turbomachinery and digital controls, it offers modular scalability, high availability, and flexible integration—air or water cooled, standalone or grid connected. With end-to-end support and bankable performance, our ORC solutions help you monetize unused heat, accelerate decarbonization, and create measurable business value from day one.

Designed for total heat inputs of approximately 2,000 to 8,000 kWth, the system primarily operates through a high‑temperature (HT) circuit, which accounts for about 90–95% of the heat input. Typical HT circuit temperatures range from 300 °C at the inlet to 240 °C at the outlet.

faqs.q: What does operational resilience mean for power plant operators today?
faqs.a: Operational resilience is the ability to maintain reliable, efficient, and flexible performance in the face of fluctuating demand, market changes, regulatory pressures, and unforeseen disruptions.

faqs.q: Why is it important for operators to strengthen the operational resiliency of their gas-fired power plants?
faqs.a: Operational resilience is the ability to maintain reliable, efficient, and flexible performance in the face of fluctuating demand, market changes, regulatory pressures, and unforeseen disruptions.

faqs.q: What do power plant operators need to do to strengthen their operational resiliency?
faqs.a: Strengthening operational resiliency requires a strategic evaluation of a plant's specific operational requirements and the prevailing market conditions. Operators must perform a comprehensive risk assessment to identify their most critical vulnerabilities and then align their resilience investments with their long-term commercial goals.

faqs.q: What is the difference between power plant reliability and power plant resilience?
faqs.a: Reliability refers to the plant’s ability to perform its intended function under normal operating conditions. Resilience, however, is the plant’s ability to withstand and adapt to changing market conditions and operational requirements.

faqs.q: How does resilient gas-fired power plant support the energy transition?
faqs.a: Resilient gas-fired power plants provide the essential flexibility and grid stability needed to balance intermittent renewables, ensuring a reliable power supply while transitioning toward carbon-neutral fuels like hydrogen.
